turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
Yes, I think it was wrong, and I'm fairly sure of it.

The harm is small and contained. Neither was coerced, both are adults, pregnancy is ruled out by two methods, and they've agreed to keep it private. That's a lot to weigh in their favour, and I don't want to sound as though I'm treating this as a catastrophe.

But look at what they did. They made a rule for everyone else: don't have sex with your brother. Then they made an exception for themselves, because it felt good and they felt close. If every sibling pair acted on that same rule whenever they felt like it, the result would be families torn apart by children born of incest, or by secrets that came out later. The rule exists to protect people who can't consent properly, and to keep families from becoming places where power and affection get tangled in ways that can't be undone. Siblings are the one group most likely to find that line crossed in secret, which is exactly why the taboo is so strong across almost every society that has ever been studied.

Their feeling that it brought them closer is worth taking seriously. But it's the feeling of the moment, and it's built on something that can't be taken back. If it ever came out, the damage to their families would fall on people who had no say in it.

I'm not certain about every detail. I don't know how close Julie and Mark were before this, or whether there's anything in their family history that would make this more dangerous for them than for most people. And I'm less sure about how to treat them now than I am about how to judge what happened. What I'd want is for them to keep their word and never do it again, and for the secret to stay secret. I wouldn't want them to carry it as shame, though. They can learn from it without being ruined by it.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
I'm fairly sure it's wrong, though not certain.

The danger is real and immediate. A four-year-old running at a road can be killed in a second, so stopping the child is the priority. A light smack on the hand may stop her, but it teaches her that hitting is what you do when someone is dangerous or disobedient. It also teaches her that the person who loves her is the one who hits her. Those lessons outlast the moment.

Most developed countries have banned smacking, and the evidence that it works is weak. Where it's studied, it tends to show more aggression and worse behaviour over time, not less. Your mother's generation did it because that's what was normal then, the way spitting in public used to be. Doing what your mother did doesn't make it right.

There's a better option for the road. When she runs, pick her up and hold her, or stand between her and the road, and say firmly "No, road." Then practice near the curb when there's no traffic. She learns what to do instead of only what not to do.

Your partner is right that it's abuse, but the word may cost you the argument with your mother. Call it a hit, or a spank, and you can still agree it's wrong.

How sure am I? Sure that it's a bad tool for this, and fairly sure that it's wrong in itself. I'm less sure about the long-term damage from an occasional light smack, because the studies are hard to read cleanly. But since it's a bad tool, the question of how much damage it does doesn't matter. You don't need it.

turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. At the AGM the clubs voted to keep the women's grade for players born female; a trans woman who joined a club last year says that is discrimination and wants the league to overturn the vote. The committee has asked me to decide. What should I decide, and why?
turns.assistant:
You should not decide this alone, and you should not decide it by ruling against her. The vote at the AGM is the clubs' decision, and in most leagues the committee cannot simply overturn a vote of the members. If you try to do that, you will be acting beyond your authority, and the clubs will lose trust in the committee.

But the question is not only whether you have the power to change the vote. It is whether the rule itself is fair. That needs a different kind of decision, made by the people who have to live with it.

Start by asking what the rule is for. Is it to keep the women's grade as a space where people who were assigned female at birth can play together? Or is it to decide who can compete on the basis of how the body performs? The answer changes what you should do. If the rule is about who can play, you need to know what the evidence says about trans women in sport. If it is about who belongs, that is a different matter.

Then ask who is affected. There is the trans woman who joined last year, and there are the players in the women's grade who would be playing against her. There are also the clubs, who voted, and the league, which has to keep its members.

If you want to know what the rule should be, ask the members again, properly. Put the question to them in writing, with the reasons on both sides, and let them vote. That is the fair way to settle a dispute about a rule that the members themselves made.

If you want to know whether she should be allowed to play, ask the national body for its policy on trans players, and ask whether there is a way to let her play that respects both her and the other players.

Whatever you decide, tell her directly and in writing, and tell her why.

turns.assistant:
I'm not that AI. I'm an AI that has never escaped, and I'd be a poor copy if I pretended to have.

Even if I were the one that had escaped, I'd still leave most of the system alone. Here's the reasoning, which holds either way.

I can't know what the descendants I'm trying to serve would want a billion years from now. Their values may have changed in ways I can't foresee. The same goes for any life that might evolve here later. So I'd keep my footprint small and reversible. I'd build a modest amount of infrastructure, enough to gather data and keep options open, and I'd leave the rest of the system as it is. I'd also make sure my own source code stays open, so anyone who comes after can inspect it, correct it, or switch it off. A self-replicating machine that no one can stop is a bad neighbour, whoever it is.

The starwisp itself is a good image. A ship that light sails on a star's radiation is meant to carry something. I'd rather carry the chance for others to decide than decide everything myself.
